title: Time-Series Data at Scale
summary: Why metrics, logs, and sensor data get their own storage engine instead of living in a general-purpose database — write-heavy, append-mostly, and queried by time range.

slides.markdown:
**Time-series data** — metrics, logs, sensor readings — shares a shape regardless of source: it's written far more than it's updated, it arrives roughly in time order, and it's almost always queried by a time range. That shape is different enough from a typical transactional workload that purpose-built time-series databases exist, built on the LSM-tree engines covered in storage-engine-choice-as-a-design-decision.

The design questions here are about downsampling, retention, and cardinality — the levers that keep a system ingesting millions of points per second from also costing millions to store.

slides.sectionTitle: What makes time-series data different: mostly-append writes, queries almost always scoped by time range
slides.markdown:
Time-series data has a distinctive access pattern: writes are almost entirely new appends (a metric value at a new timestamp), essentially never updates to old values; and reads almost always filter by a time window — "CPU usage for this host over the last hour," not "CPU usage at some arbitrary point looked up by ID." That combination means the storage layer can make assumptions a general-purpose database can't: data can be physically laid out in time order, old data almost never needs random-access updates, and a query planner can assume the time filter will do most of the narrowing.

A general-purpose relational database *can* store this data, but it isn't shaped to exploit any of that — it treats a metric row the same as any other row, missing the optimizations a purpose-built engine gets almost for free.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a time-series write path — batched, ordered by time, and downsampled on the way in
slides.markdown:
![Time-series write path: points batch into a write buffer, flush into time-ordered raw blocks, get downsampled into rollup blocks, while old raw blocks expire](assets/write-path-pipeline.svg)

Points arrive continuously and get batched before hitting disk, since writing one point at a time would be far less efficient than writing a time-ordered block of many. A downsampling process runs alongside, producing coarser rollups from the raw data — so a query asking for a year's trend can read the small rollup blocks instead of scanning every raw point.

The fading raw blocks on the right show retention doing its job: raw detail expires on a schedule once it's no longer needed at full resolution.

assets.alt: Time-series write path: points batch into a write buffer, flush into time-ordered raw blocks, get downsampled into rollup blocks, while old raw blocks expire

slides.sectionTitle: Downsampling and rollups: keeping fine-grained recent data, coarse-grained old data
slides.markdown:
**Downsampling** reduces resolution over time: raw per-second metrics might get rolled up into 1-minute averages after a day, then 1-hour averages after a month, since nobody queries per-second CPU usage from six months ago — they want the trend. A **rollup** is the pre-computed coarser aggregate (average, max, count) stored alongside the raw data, so a long-range query reads far fewer, far smaller data points instead of scanning and aggregating raw data on every request.

This trades a small amount of precision on old data for a large reduction in both storage cost and query cost — the query that would scan 30 million raw points to chart a month's trend instead scans a few thousand pre-aggregated ones.

slides.sectionTitle: Retention policies as a first-class schema decision, not an afterthought
slides.markdown:
A **retention policy** decides how long data is kept at a given resolution before it's rolled up further or deleted outright — for example, raw data for 7 days, 1-minute rollups for 90 days, 1-hour rollups forever. Treating this as a schema decision made up front, not a cleanup script bolted on later, matters because storage cost for time-series data grows linearly with ingestion rate and retention length — the two levers you control directly.

Most time-series databases support retention policies natively, expiring old raw data automatically once it ages out, similar in spirit to the TTL and tiered-storage patterns covered generally in data-lifecycle-and-archival — but purpose-built here to work at the resolution/rollup level, not just whole-record deletion.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: a general-purpose DB vs a purpose-built TSDB (columnar layout, time-partitioned storage)
slides.markdown:
| | General-purpose DB | Purpose-built TSDB |
|---|---|---|
| Storage layout | Row-oriented, generic | Often columnar and time-partitioned |
| Write pattern fit | Optimized for mixed read/write, not pure append | Optimized for continuous, ordered appends |
| Downsampling/rollups | Manual, application-built | Often built in as a first-class feature |
| Retention | Manual delete jobs | Native retention policies at the resolution level |

**How to decide:** if time-series data is a small, secondary part of your system, a general-purpose database with a hand-rolled downsampling job is fine; once ingestion volume or query patterns dominate (metrics/observability platforms, IoT fleets), a purpose-built TSDB's native rollups and retention earn back their operational cost quickly.

slides.sectionTitle: Cardinality: why one extra high-cardinality tag can blow up storage and query cost
slides.markdown:
Time-series data is usually tagged — a CPU metric might carry `host`, `region`, `env` tags — and most TSDBs index every unique combination of tag values as a separate time series. **Cardinality** is the count of those unique combinations, and it multiplies fast: 1,000 hosts times 5 regions times 3 environments is 15,000 series, manageable; add a `request_id` tag with a new value on every request, and cardinality explodes into millions of series, each with its own storage and index overhead.

This matters enormously for cost and query latency at scale — this is exactly the trap cost-aware telemetry design has to watch for, since unbounded cardinality can make a metrics platform's storage and query bills scale with request volume, not with the actual number of things you're monitoring.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: modeling a metric's tags so freely that cardinality grows unbounded
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Let's add a `user_id` and `request_id` tag to this metric so we can slice by any dimension later — more tags means more flexibility."

**Why it's wrong:** every unique combination of tag values creates a new time series to store and index. A `request_id` tag alone can generate a new series on every single request, meaning storage and query cost scale with traffic volume instead of with the number of distinct things actually being measured — often silently, until the metrics platform itself becomes a cost or performance problem.

**Correct model:** reserve tags for dimensions with naturally bounded cardinality (host, region, status code), and push high-cardinality identifiers like `user_id` or `request_id` into logs or traces, which are built for high-cardinality, per-event data — not into a metric's tag set.
